components.label: kutch-ajrakh/design/cloth-field-and-borders-photo
components.title: An ajrakh held up to show its field and borders
components.description: The masthead photograph: two Kutch artisans hold up a whole ajrakh so its repeated central field, borders and end panels show, under a label card naming Kutch Ajrakh, Kachchh and its GI registration of 22 April 2024. Place it at the head of a Kutch Ajrakh page or wherever the cloth's fixed layout of field, borders and end panels is described.

components.label: shared/chemistry/indigo-vat-dip
components.title: Green from the vat, blue in the air
components.description: Fig. 1: an animated pit vat in which a resist-printed cloth is dipped, lifted bright green and turns blue in the air, with a three-phase strip, a Dip again control that deepens the blue over up to four dips, and the balanced equation 2 leucoindigo + O2 → 2 indigo + 2 H2O with an atom count. Place it wherever a page explains why indigo-dyed cloth leaves the vat green and turns blue; the cloth is drawn with ajrakh's gach resist, but the chemistry holds for any indigo vat craft.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/at-a-glance
components.title: At a glance
components.description: An eight-line fact list for Kutch Ajrakh: centres, makers and wearers, colours, dyes and mordants, number of stages, time per piece, resists, and one-sided ek-puri against double-sided bi-puri cloth. Place it near the start of a Kutch Ajrakh page as a quick orientation before the detailed chapters.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/design/indigo-ground-specimen
components.title: Stars on an indigo ground
components.description: A full-width photograph of an ajrakh detail, dark eight-pointed stars and white-outlined motifs on an indigo ground, with a specimen label card and a Dip it again control that tints the photograph vat-green and lets it return to blue. Place it where a page shows what an ajrakh looks like close up, or as a lead-in to the indigo dip of Fig. 1.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/four-colours-four-chemistries
components.title: One cloth, four chemistries
components.description: Four cards, one per ajrakh colour, blue vadali, black kalo, red laal and white safed, each with a before-and-after swatch pair and the agent that makes it: indigo then air, iron on tannin, madder on alum, and lime that keeps the white. Place it where a page explains why ajrakh needs all four colours and how each is fixed.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/design/indigo-ground-print-photo
components.title: Ajrak print in blue, black and white
components.description: A tall photograph of an indigo-ground ajrak printed with star and lattice motifs, set beside short notes on the cloth itself (cotton of 60s to 120s count, silk to order) and on what the four colours mean. Place it where a page discusses ajrakh's cloth, its pattern or the meaning of its colours.

components.label: shared/process/printing-block-carving-photo
components.title: A textile printing block being carved
components.description: A photograph of a craftsman holding up a wooden textile printing block carved with floral and roundel motifs at the Anokhi Museum, Jaipur, in December 2019, captioned as a Jaipur block, not an ajrakh block. Place it on any hand block printing page where block carving or the printer's tools are described, keeping that caution.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/process/cloth-after-each-stage
components.title: One cloth, drawn after each stage
components.description: Fig. 2: a stage player that draws one ajrakh cloth after each of eleven stages, saaj to minakari, with a ribbon of stage tiles and a Play the stages control; each stage gives its native and English names, what it does, why, the cloth's colour after and its materials with local and botanical names. Place it wherever the making sequence of Kutch Ajrakh is told; other chapters link to its stages.

components.label: shared/chemistry/indigo-reduction-player
components.title: The blue starts colourless in the leaf, dissolves in the vat and returns in the air
components.description: Fig. 3: a four-step reaction player from leaf to fibre: β-glucosidase frees indoxyl from indican, two indoxyl join into indigo, the vat reduces indigo to soluble leucoindigo, and air oxidises it back to blue. Each step has structures drawn from PubChem, a balanced equation with an atom count, and its conditions. Place it on any indigo-dyed craft's page that explains the vat.

components.label: shared/chemistry/indican-indigo-leucoindigo-3d
components.title: Indigo and leucoindigo differ by two hydrogen atoms
components.description: Fig. 4: three turnable 3D models from PubChem conformers, indican from the leaf, indigo and leucoindigo, with formulas, CIDs and the oxygens that gain or lose a hydrogen ringed. Place it beside any explanation of indigo's reduction in the vat and oxidation in air.

components.label: shared/chemistry/indigo-leaf-to-cloth-chain
components.title: Where the blue comes from, and back
components.description: A six-link chain from the indigo leaf to the cake, natural or German indigo, the vat, the cloth and back round the cycle, with a balanced hydros vat equation (indigo, sodium dithionite and caustic soda giving the soluble sodium salt of leucoindigo) and its inferred steps marked. Place it where a page needs the whole life of indigo dye in one compact diagram rather than the step player.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/indoxyl-to-indigo-hypothesis
components.title: The source's own words for step 2
components.description: A small card showing a source's wording of indigo formation, indoxyl plus air giving indigo, marked Hypothesis because its carbons (8 before, 16 after) do not balance, and pointing to the balanced form in Fig. 3. Place it only beside the indigo reduction player, where it shows how the page handles a source equation that does not balance.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/red-alum-madder-player
components.title: Red develops only where alum was printed, and lime takes the alum away
components.description: Fig. 5: a five-step player on one printed square of cotton: harde puts tannin in, pa prints alum, lime in the outline removes the alum, madder or alizarin is heated in, and alizarin locks onto aluminium as a red lake in the fibre; each step lists its species with PubChem CIDs. Place it where a page explains ajrakh's red or mordant dyeing with alum.

components.label: shared/chemistry/alizarin-purpurin-3d
components.title: Madder's red is more than alizarin
components.description: Fig. 6: turnable 3D models of alizarin and purpurin from PubChem conformers, with purpurin's extra hydroxyl ringed, beside notes that synthetic alizarin is the same molecule as madder's, that it was first made in 1868, and that Indian madder holds both. Place it on any madder- or alizarin-dyed craft's page.

components.label: shared/materials/madder-roots-and-dyed-silk-photo
components.title: Madder roots beside madder-dyed silk
components.description: A photograph of thin brown madder roots in a clay bowl beside red and pink skeins of madder-dyed tasar silk, captioned as tasar silk, not ajrakh, with a note that ajrakh's red is extracted from these long thin roots of Indian madder and links to the alum mordant. Place it where a page introduces madder as a dye material.

components.label: shared/chemistry/alizarin-aluminium-ring-structures
components.title: Alizarin closes a six-member ring on aluminium
components.description: Fig. 7: 2D structures of alizarin and purpurin as the compound library draws them, marking the six-member ring alizarin closes on an aluminium ion and the third hydroxyl purpurin adds, with atom counts and PubChem CIDs. Place it where a page explains how an alum mordant holds a madder or alizarin red.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/iron-tannin-black-player
components.title: Iron printed on tannin turns chocolate-black, and iron in the wash water spots the cloth
components.description: Fig. 8: a four-step player for ajrakh's black: harde puts tannic acid in the cotton, scrap iron ferments into iron acetate for the kut paste, the printed iron(II) oxidises to iron(III) that the tannin holds as black, and iron in the wash water leaves black spots; balanced equations carry atom and charge counts. Place it where a page explains iron-tannin black or iron in dye water.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/white-resist-player
components.title: White is cloth the dye never reached
components.description: Fig. 9: a five-step player for ajrakh's white: saaj scouring in castor oil, soda ash and camel dung, lime and gum outlines, the gach resist of clay and millet flour, gentle washing in running water and a cool morning wash that keeps the alum. Place it where a page explains resist printing or how ajrakh keeps its whites.

components.label: shared/chemistry/indigo-in-cotton-fibre-explainer
components.title: Inside one cotton fibre: the vat, then the air
components.description: Fig. 10: a model-built explainer in a sealed frame whose time slider follows one cotton fibre through the vat, the dip, the lift and the air, counting leucoindigo, indigo, oxygen used and water made, drawn from the five cited sentences listed beneath it. Place it where a reader wants the fibre-scale picture of indigo dyeing; it pictures the claims and is not a measurement.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/materials/six-materials
components.title: Six materials
components.description: Six cards for the dyes, mordants and resist behind ajrakh's colours, indigo, madder, alum, kut, harde and lime, each with the name printers use, the botanical name where it is a plant, its compound's formula and PubChem CID, and a cited fact. Place it where a page lists what ajrakh is made from.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/materials/natural-dye-materials-photo
components.title: Labelled bags of dye and printing materials
components.description: A photograph of hand-labelled bags of powders, roots and crystals laid on an ajrakh, with lime and alum in the left columns and alizarin and madder powder in the right, beside the GI journal's full list of ajrakh's ingredients. Place it with a materials list or wherever the reader should see the raw dyes and mordants.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/process/experts-differ
components.title: Experts differ
components.description: Six places where two sources give different readings of ajrakh's process, each quoting both: how the vat is reduced, how long the natural vat and the kut iron ferment, how long the red bath lasts, the metal of the red pot and how often saaj is repeated, with two range charts. Place it where a page should show that its sources disagree rather than pick one reading.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/process/kut-fermenting-days-range
components.title: Ten to fifteen days, or one to two weeks by season
components.description: Fig. 11: a range chart of how long the iron for kut ferments, the GI journal's 10 to 15 days against Clifford's one week in the hot season and two in the cold, with the gap between them hatched. Place it beside the kut stage or the chemistry of ajrakh's black.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/process/red-bath-hours-range
components.title: Two to three hours, or up to four
components.description: Fig. 12: a range chart of the red dye bath's length, Karolia and Buch's 2 to 3 hours against the GI journal's up to 4 for the purest reds, with the gap hatched. Place it beside the rang stage or the chemistry of ajrakh's red.

components.label: shared/geography/great-rann-of-kachchh-photo
components.title: The Great Rann of Kachchh
components.description: A chapter-opening photograph of the white salt flat of the Great Rann of Kachchh under a clear sky, captioned as salt flat, not sea, and not Dhamadka or Ajrakhpur; the anchored opener also holds the Why Kachchh chapter's number, heading and dek over the photo. Place it at the head of any section on Kachchh's land and water.

components.label: shared/climate/kachchh-district-climate-map
components.title: Kachchh is the fourth driest of these 27 districts, and its rain is rising
components.description: Fig. 13: a district map of Kachchh and the 26 districts around it in Gujarat and Rajasthan with four layers, rainfall, rain trend, temperature and soil pH, three zooms from India to the three ajrakh villages, keyboard reading and a ranked list of all 27 values. Place it on any Kachchh craft's page where climate, water or soil explains the craft.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/geography/suran-earthquake-ajrakhpur-cards
components.title: The Suran, the earthquake and the move to Ajrakhpur
components.description: Fig. 14: eight dated cards on the same stretch of Kachchh. The first four carry a small map: the Suran flowing north into the Banni, the stream drying in 1989, the 2001 earthquake and iron in the water, and the move 40 km to Ajrakhpur; then come deeper wells (a depth diagram), effluent treatment and Barmer and Sindh (stat tiles), and the same iron doing two jobs (two swatches). Place it where a page tells why ajrakh's water and villages changed.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/geography/suran-flowing-north-map
components.anchor: [aria-label="The Suran flowing north past Dhamadka into the Banni"]
components.title: The Suran flowing north past Dhamadka
components.description: A small map from Fig. 14 of the Suran flowing north past Dhamadka into the Banni until the late 1980s, unlike other Kachchh rivers, which flow south. Place it where a page describes Dhamadka's river before the dam.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/geography/suran-dry-below-tapar-dam-map
components.anchor: [aria-label="The Suran dry below the dam at Tapar"]
components.title: The Suran dry below the dam at Tapar
components.description: A small map from Fig. 14 showing the Suran dry below the upstream dam at Tapar after Dhamadka's stream dried in 1989. Place it where a page describes Dhamadka losing its river water.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/geology/dhamadka-epicentre-circle-map
components.title: A 20 km circle around Dhamadka
components.description: A small map from Fig. 14 with a 20 km circle around Dhamadka, the distance the sources give to the epicentre of the 2001 earthquake that almost destroyed the village and left more iron in its water. Place it where a page tells what the earthquake did to ajrakh.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/history/dhamadka-to-ajrakhpur-move-map
components.anchor: [aria-label="An arrow from Dhamadka west to Ajrakhpur, 40 km"]
components.title: Forty kilometres to Ajrakhpur
components.description: A small map from Fig. 14 with an arrow from Dhamadka west to Ajrakhpur, 40 km, the village founded in May 2001 for Dhamadka's printers in search of better groundwater. Place it where a page tells the move to Ajrakhpur.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/geology/ajrakhpur-borewell-depth
components.title: The wells go deeper
components.description: A depth diagram drawn to scale from 0 to 500 ft: water once rose at 200 feet below ground at Ajrakhpur, and a later private borewell had to reach 450 feet. Place it where a page discusses Ajrakhpur's falling water table.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/ecology/effluent-treatment-stats
components.title: Treating the water
components.description: Two stat tiles: a pilot effluent treatment plant Khamir set up in 2007, and a Rs 1.5 crore effluent system opened at Ajrakhpur in 2022. Place it where a page discusses dye effluent and water recycling at Ajrakhpur.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/geography/lower-sindh-ajrak-survey-stats
components.title: Barmer and Sindh
components.description: Three stat tiles from Bilgrami's two-year survey of Lower Sindh, published in 1990: 21 stages, 15 centres and 78 master craftsmen of ajrak. Place it where a page compares Kachchh ajrakh with Sindh's.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/iron-on-purpose-and-by-accident
components.title: The same iron, two jobs
components.description: Two myrobalan-yellow swatches, one with a black printed star and one with small black spots: iron prints ajrakh's black on purpose in stage 5 and spots the cloth by accident from the wash water, with a link to stage 5 in Fig. 2. Place it where a page connects the black's chemistry to Kachchh's iron-rich water.

components.label: shared/climate/kachchh-annual-rainfall-chart
components.title: Rain over Kachchh has risen about 71 mm a decade since 1981
components.description: Fig. 15: a bar chart of annual rainfall over Kachchh district from CHIRPS 3.0, 1981 to 2025, around a mean of 449 mm, with a Theil–Sen trend of +70.8 mm a decade, the extremes of 69 and 844 mm, four lettered ajrakh water events (1989, 2001, 2007, 2022), keyboard reading and a table and CSV of all 45 values. Place it on any Kachchh craft's page about rain or water.

components.label: shared/climate/kachchh-annual-temperature-chart
components.title: Kachchh has also warmed, about 0.3 °C a decade
components.description: Fig. 16: a chart of annual mean air temperature over Kachchh district from GHCN-CAMS, 1981 to 2025, with a Theil–Sen trend of +0.30 °C a decade. Place it on any Kachchh craft's page about heat or climate.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/geography/bhuj-ajrakhpur-dhamadka-distances
components.title: Ajrakhpur is 12 km from Bhuj; the sources put Dhamadka 50 or 60 km away
components.description: Fig. 17: a distance diagram placing Ajrakhpur 12 km from Bhuj and 40 km from Dhamadka, and Dhamadka about 50 km from Bhuj in the GI journal or 60 km in Karolia and Buch. Place it where a page locates the ajrakh villages relative to Bhuj.

components.label: shared/geography/banni-grasslands-photo
components.title: The Banni grasslands
components.description: A photograph of dry, cracked ground in the Banni grasslands of Kachchh in April 2016, captioned as the Banni, not Dhamadka, beside a pull quote from Khamir on the Dhamadka river that emptied into the Banni instead of flowing south. Place it where a page describes Kachchh's dry land or its rivers.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/geography/why-here
components.title: The ground under Kutch Ajrakh
components.description: A map of where Kutch Ajrakh is practised over relief, rivers and recorded mineral deposits, with each place's measured ground beside it.

components.label: shared/history/mohenjo-daro-priest-king-trefoil
components.title: The priest-king bust of Mohenjo-daro
components.description: A photograph of the Mohenjo-daro priest-king bust, its shawl carved with the trefoil that block printers read as kakar, the cloud motif of ajrakh, captioned to make the reader look at the trefoils. Place it where a page discusses ajrakh's claimed antiquity or the kakar motif.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/history/dated-record-timeline-map
components.title: Ajrakh's dated record runs from the Fustat cloths to a 2024 registration
components.description: Fig. 18: a timeline on a twice-broken axis linked to a map; pressing a moment or Play draws the line between the places its dated sentence names, from Mohenjo-daro and Al Fustat through the king's invitation of 1586 to 1631, the V&A, alizarin in 1868 and the 2001 earthquake to the 2024 GI, and a switch adds material sources. Place it where a page tells ajrakh's history and trade.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/economics/dhamadka-yardage-2014
components.title: In 2014 a Dhamadka workshop's cotton yardage for Fabindia ran to 70,000 m
components.description: Fig. 19: a two-bar chart of Abduljabbar M. Khatri's 2014 production as Edwards reports it, 70,000 m of cotton running yardage for Fabindia, New Delhi, against 1,000 m for Maiwa, Vancouver. Place it where a page discusses ajrakh's move from caste dress to urban yardage.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/policy/gi-registration-card
components.title: Kutch Ajrakh, geographical indication, application 1050
components.description: A label card for Kutch Ajrakh's geographical indication: application 1050, a seal, the four-colour rule, the application-to-certificate timeline of Fig. 20, and its proprietor (Ajarakhpur Hastkala Vikas Sangathan), goods (classes 24 and 25) and facilitator (the Textiles Committee). Place it where a page covers ajrakh's legal protection.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/policy/gi-application-to-certificate
components.title: From application to certificate took 447 days
components.description: Fig. 20: a three-point timeline of the Kutch Ajrakh GI: application on 31 January 2023, publication in the GI journal on 19 December 2023 after 322 days, and the certificate on 22 April 2024 after 125 more. Place it where a page needs the GI's dates on their own.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/what-if-lab
components.title: What if the dyer changed one thing?
components.description: Fig. 21: an experiment lab of three choices the sources describe, each shown with what follows: setting the vat with natural indigo or with hydros and caustic soda, dyeing the red with madder root or synthetic alizarin, and washing in water carrying alum or iron. The blue panel has a days chart, the red a swatch and an hours chart, the water a swatch; the blue and red panels carry formula chips. Place it where a page invites the reader to compare traditional and modern choices.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/what-if-indigo-vat
components.title: Set the vat with natural indigo, or hydros and caustic soda
components.description: The blue vat experiment of Fig. 21: switch between a living natural indigo vat that takes a month or months to set and a chemical hydros vat ready in 3 to 4 days, with the cited consequences, a days chart and formula chips for indigo, sodium dithionite and caustic soda. Place it where a page compares fermentation and chemical reduction of indigo.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/process/vat-setting-days
components.anchor: [aria-label="Days to set a vat: 3 to 4 for a hydros vat; about one month, or months, for a natural vat"]
components.title: A hydros vat is ready in 3 to 4 days; a natural vat takes about a month, or months
components.description: A small range chart from Fig. 21 of the days needed to set an indigo vat, 3 to 4 for a hydros vat against about one month, or months, for a natural vat, with the span between the two sources hatched. Place it beside a comparison of natural and chemical indigo vats.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/what-if-red-dye
components.title: Dye the red with madder root, or synthetic alizarin
components.description: The red bath experiment of Fig. 21: switch between madder root, which leaves a pink cast on the whites that tapano bleaches, and synthetic alizarin, with a swatch, a day-by-day tapano control, a switch that lets the pa touch the lime outline, an hours chart and formula chips for alizarin, purpurin and alum. Place it where a page compares natural madder and synthetic alizarin.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/process/red-bath-hours
components.anchor: [aria-label="Hours in the red bath: 2 to 3 in Karolia and Buch, up to 4 for the purest reds in the GI journal"]
components.title: The red bath: 2 to 3 hours, or up to 4 for the purest reds
components.description: A small range chart from Fig. 21 of hours in the red bath, 2 to 3 in Karolia and Buch and up to 4 in the GI journal, the disagreement hatched; the same readings as Fig. 12, drawn for the lab. Place it beside the red dyeing stage.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/what-if-wash-water
components.title: Wash the myrobalan-yellow cloth in water with alum, or with iron
components.description: The wash water experiment of Fig. 21: wash myrobalan-yellow cloth in water carrying alum, tin or chrome, which brightens colours, or iron, which dulls them and leaves black spots, with a swatch and a link to the same iron printing the black. Place it where a page explains how water quality affects dyed colour.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/society/khavda-khatris-2011-dots
components.title: 45 Khatris in Khavda in 2011, 15 of them on ajrakh
components.description: A dot chart of the 45 Khatris still in Khavda in 2011, 15 of them working on ajrakh, all with chemical dyes. Place it where a page discusses who still prints ajrakh and how few remain in Khavda.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/design/printer-hand-at-border-photo
components.title: A printer's hand at the edge of an ajrakh
components.description: A cropped photograph of an artisan's hand at the edge of a printed ajrakh, beside the bands of border print that frame its central field. Place it where a page discusses the printers or ajrakh's borders.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/society/sufian-khatri-iron-water-voice
components.title: In the artisan's words
components.description: A published-testimony card quoting Sufian Khatri, a ninth-generation ajrakh craftsman, to Mongabay India in 2019: even one percent iron in the wash water spots the myrobalan-yellow cloth black, with a second voice from Khamir's Ajrakh exhibition saying the same. Place it where a page needs the printers' own account of iron in the water.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/related-crafts
components.title: Related crafts
components.description: Four cards linking Kutch Ajrakh to monographs that share a material or method, Bagru Hand Block Print, Sanganeri Hand Block Printing, Machilipatnam Kalamkari and Bagh Prints of Madhya Pradesh, each with the linking sentence and a swatch of the ajrakh stage they share, drawn as in Fig. 2. Place it near the end of a page to lead readers to kin crafts.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/shared-science-atlas
components.title: The same science, named in other monographs
components.description: Six concept groups, indigo, madder, alum, lime, mordant and tannin, each counting the monographs and Kutch Ajrakh sentences that name it and the concepts named beside it, leading with the craft that names it most and a Show all of every craft's sentence. Place it where a page shows how ajrakh's materials and chemistry recur across crafts.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/society/coda-printer-on-water
components.title: Coda: in the printer's words
components.description: A closing quote card over a drawing of the ajrakh as it leaves stage 11, minakari: Sufian Khatri telling Mongabay India in 2019 that water and good quality water is essential to the survival of ajrakh. Place it at the end of a Kutch Ajrakh page.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/how-to-read-citations
components.title: Every numeral opens a source
components.description: A worked example of the page's citations: one cited sentence on the 2001 earthquake, keys a to d for the source numerals, the source's exact words, where they sit and the A to D reliability grade, beside the two source cards it opens. Place it once per page among the reading tools.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/listen
components.title: Listen
components.description: A read-aloud control that opens the page's player bar: the short answer and each chapter's opening read in about 7 minutes, the sentence being read marked and followed, with previous, next and speed controls. Place it among a page's reading tools.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/check-yourself-quiz
components.title: Check yourself
components.description: A three-question quiz in which each blank was a word in one of the answer's cited sentences and every choice opens the sentence it comes from, ending with a score. Place it near the end of a page so a reader can test what they read.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/ask-next
components.title: Ask next
components.description: Six follow-up questions that pick up where the sources stop, on keeping the indigo vat working, the stages after phulli, groundwater salinity, saponification in saaj, the bio-water effluent plant and why lime discharges alum, each starting a new answer at the same depth. Place it at the end of a page.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/cite-this-page
components.title: Cite this page
components.description: A citation box with tabs for this answer and for the monograph, citation styles (APA, BibTeX, text, link) and a copy button, noting that version 1 stays at its address. Place it among a page's reading tools.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/answer-in-hindi-and-urdu
components.title: In हिन्दी and اردو
components.description: A language switch that shows the answer's opening and its first section, on the chemistry, in Hindi or Urdu with the same source numerals and margin; the Hindi panel also carries a Hindi figure of alizarin and purpurin and the masthead photograph with a Hindi caption. Place it among a page's reading tools for readers who prefer Hindi or Urdu.

components.label: shared/chemistry/alizarin-purpurin-structures-hindi
components.title: Alizarin and purpurin, madder's reds, in Hindi
components.description: The Hindi figure of alizarin and purpurin: 2D structures marking the six-member ring alizarin closes on aluminium and purpurin's third hydroxyl, with Hindi captions, cited Hindi sentences and swatches of white under lime and pink where madder reached. Place it in Hindi text about madder or an alum-mordant red.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/student-version
components.title: The student version
components.description: An expandable rewrite of the indigo dip for a reader of 14 to 17, in seven short cited sentences: why indigo needs a vat, how bacteria turn it into soluble leucoindigo, and why the cloth comes out green and turns blue. Place it where a page offers a simpler reading of the indigo chemistry.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/indigo-dip-story-panels
components.title: The answer as six story panels
components.description: Six AI-illustrated story panels, each labelled AI and captioned with a cited sentence, telling the indigo dip from the Kachchh villages and the naand dug into the ground to bacteria in the vat, the green cloth turning blue and repeated dips. Place it where a younger or general reader needs the indigo story in pictures.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/watch-it-being-made
components.title: Each section arrives with its picture
components.description: A replay of the answer being written section by section, with an Illustrate as I write switch, a progress bar and a media rail, as each of the seven sections arrives with its AI illustration, then a short AI video and the AI film. Place it where a page shows how an Expert answer and its media were made.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/ai-cloth-lifted-from-vat
components.title: Cloth lifted from the vat, green at the hem and blue at the top
components.description: An AI illustration, labelled AI and not a photograph, of cloth lifted from the vat, green at the hem and blue at the top, drawn from the chemistry section's sentence on oxidation in air, with a download. Place it beside text on the indigo dip when no photograph is wanted.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/chemistry/ai-video-blue-in-the-air
components.title: Blue in the air
components.description: An 8-second silent AI video, labelled AI and not a recording, of cloth rising out of the vat bright green and turning blue from the top down, the dip of Fig. 1 in motion, with play, scrub and download. Place it beside the indigo dip when motion helps.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/history/ai-caravan-on-salt-flat
components.title: A caravan crossing a salt flat at dawn
components.description: An AI illustration, labelled AI and not a photograph, of a caravan crossing a salt flat at dawn, drawn from the history section's sentence on Khatri printers invited from Sindh to Kutch, with a download. Place it beside text on ajrakh's migration from Sindh.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/design/ai-double-sided-ajrakh-drying
components.title: An ajrakh drying on a line
components.description: An AI illustration, labelled AI and not a photograph, of an ajrakh drying on a line with a corner turned to show the same print behind, drawn from the sentence that the most prized cloths were printed identically on both sides, with a download. Place it beside text on double-sided bi-puri printing.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/geography/ai-dry-riverbed-and-well
components.title: A dry riverbed beside a stone well
components.description: An AI illustration, labelled AI and not a photograph, of a dry riverbed beside a stone well, drawn from the geography section's sentences on the Suran drying and iron in Dhamadka's water, with a download. Place it beside text on ajrakh's water story.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/economics/ai-stacked-printed-yardage
components.title: Folded lengths of printed cloth
components.description: An AI illustration, labelled AI and not a photograph, of folded lengths of printed cloth stacked on a table, drawn from the economics section's sentence on barter with herders, with a download. Place it beside text on ajrakh's market and yardage.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/design/ai-block-divided-into-sixteen
components.title: A block divided into four and then sixteen
components.description: An AI illustration, labelled AI and not a photograph, of a carved block whose square is divided into four and then sixteen, drawn from the design section's sentence on mizan, balance and order, with a download. Place it beside text on ajrakh's design grid.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/process/ai-cloth-steeping-in-saaj
components.title: A cloth bundle steeping overnight
components.description: An AI illustration, labelled AI and not a photograph, of a cloth bundle in hessian weighed down by a stone and steeping overnight, drawn from the process section's sentence on saaj scouring, with a download. Place it beside text on preparing the cloth.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/answer-as-a-film
components.title: The answer as a film
components.description: A 56-second AI film, labelled AI video with AI music and sound, of seven scenes, one per section of the answer, subtitled with a cited sentence from each, with a scene strip and downloads of the film and its subtitles. Place it where a page offers the whole answer as a short film.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/how-this-answer-was-made
components.title: How this answer was made
components.description: A replayable record of how the answer was made: the question understood, 44 sources read with their grades, the seven sections written with the figure each drew, and every quote checked against its source, with a Watch it being made button. Place it in a page's sources chapter to show provenance.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/source-list
components.title: Every source, numbered once
components.description: The numbered list of the answer's 44 sources in groups (government records, scholarship, museums and references, community and press, compound records), each with its grade, the sentences it supports and a link; pressing one lights those sentences. The anchor is the list's live status line, an empty element just before the list, because the list's own wrapper repeats in the kin-crafts list. Place it at the end of a page.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/kin-craft-sources
components.title: For the kin crafts
components.description: A collapsible list of the 24 sources that support only the other monographs' sentences quoted in the kin crafts chapter, counted apart from the answer's 44. Place it after the main source list whenever kin-craft sentences are shown.

components.label: kutch-ajrakh/overview/picture-and-data-credits
components.title: Pictures and data

children: A wide morning view of a Kachchh village: round huts and thorn trees on a flat horizon, long blue-and-red cloths drying on the ground, a printer stirring a vat. In front, the reader raises a hand and asks how indigo turns blue.
The printer and the reader hold a printed cloth between them and lower it together into a vat set in the ground. A clock marks ten to fifteen minutes.

Seen through a big lens inside the vat: rod-shaped bacteria cling to dark grains of indigo beside cotton fibres, and on the other side of an arrow the grains are gone, dissolved. The reader peers in, mouth open.
Hands lift the cloth out of the vat. It drips bright green at the bottom and has turned blue from the top down, as pairs of oxygen atoms drift in from the air. The reader throws up both hands.
Four cloths hang on a line, each a deeper blue than the last, tagged one to four. The reader counts them off on their fingers.
Payoff: by a stream, the printer and the reader hold up the finished ajrakh between them, deep blue with red stars and borders. Water drips from it clear, and the blue stays.

shell:
Expert answer

Kutch Ajrakh

The short answer

Ajrakh works as an elaborate resist block-printing technique: the cloth goes through a series of direct and resist printing and dyeing steps, combining hand block printing with resist dyeing. The tannin in myrobalan penetrates the cotton fibres as an essential pre-mordant, which aids the adhesion of the mordants printed on afterwards. On that treated cloth, the iron in the kut paste, oxidised by the air, binds the tannic acid into a deep, fast chocolate-black, while madder dye links to the alum mordant and develops red where the pa and gach pastes were printed.

Drawn from 44 sourcesA 28B 11C 524 more for the kin craftsAnswered 18 Nov 2026

The answer in seven sections

Chemistry, history, overview, geography, economics, design and process. Each opens the chapter of this page that tells it in full.

  1. 3Tannin, iron and alum make the colours hold
  2. 5From Sindh to Kutch at a king's invitation
  3. 2Blue, red, black and white, printed both sides
  4. 4When the river died and the iron rose
  5. 6From barter with herders to running yardage
  6. 1Balance, order and the priest-king's cloud motif
  7. 2Camel dung, myrobalan and lime prepare the cloth

UnderstoodKutch Ajrakh, at Expert depth, in English.

Answered from six angles: artisan, chemist, historian, anthropologist, economist and technologist.

The monograph

Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique of direct and resist printing and dyeing, made by Khatri artisans as a double-sided textile. Its tradition is kept up in the Kutch villages of Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda, and its process and designs are common to Sindh, where it originated, and to Barmer district of Rajasthan. A traditional piece needs all four colours, blue, black, red and white, and the most highly prized cloths were printed identically on both sides.

  • 1GI Journal No. 188: Kutch Ajrakh, 2023
  • 2Ajrakh: Rhythm of Blues
  • 7Ajarkh, the resist printed fabric of Gujarat, 2008
  • 11Ajrakh: From Caste Dress to Catwalk, 2016
  • 12AJRAKH- A Textile Tradition in Transition, 2016
  • 13Indigo in Kutch, India, 2024

The cloth itself

Ajrakh is printed mostly on cotton, in natural dyes; printers buy cotton of 60s to 120s count, by what the cloth will become, and print silk ajrakh to order.

What the colours mean

In Karolia and Buch, vadali or neela is blue, the sky; laal is red, the light of sunset; safed or dhodo is white, the stars; and kalo is black, the dark night.

Sources differ on what the colours mean
The GI application reads ajrakh's palette as the universe, with red for the earth, black for darkness, white for clouds and blue for the universe.
2

2

How it is made

Blue, red, black and white, printed both sides

Sources count 14, 15 to 16 or 16 stages, and the GI journal gives approximately 15 to 21 days for the whole process.

Ajrakh is also described as a water-intensive 16-stage process, with one step done each day before the cloth is rested.

  • 1GI Journal No. 188: Kutch Ajrakh, 2023
  • 7Ajarkh, the resist printed fabric of Gujarat, 2008
  • 15Traditional Indian textile designs for new markets (MA thesis), 2012
  • 16Water woes: Kutch's age-old Ajrakh craft, 2019
3

3

The chemistry

Tannin, iron and alum make the colours hold

Madder and synthetic alizarin both need alum as a mordant to develop red, and lime in the outline resist discharges the alum. The blue that appears in the air in Fig. 1 is followed here to its molecules, with the black and the red. Water rich in alum, tin or chrome brightens the colours, while iron in the water supply dulls and darkens the final result.

Synthetic alizarin and madder: both readings hold

Edwards writes that synthetic alizarin and German indigo are chemically identical to the natural dyestuffs. The GI journal finds the colour compounds of natural madder roots much more complex than those of synthetic alizarin, so madder often leaves a pinkish tinge on the whites. Madder holds alizarin and also purpurin, as the GI records for Bagru and Sanganeri prints state.

  • 1GI Journal No. 188: Kutch Ajrakh, 2023
  • 11Ajrakh: From Caste Dress to Catwalk, 2016
  • 18GI Journal No. 37: Bagru Hand Block Print, 2011
  • 19Application for Registration of a Geographical Indication: Sanganeri Hand Block Printing (Form GI-1 with statement of case)
  1. Blue
  2. Red
  3. Black
  4. White
  5. The vat, up close
  6. Six materials
  7. Experts differ

Blue, from leaf to fibre

Unlike most natural dyes, indigo needs no mordant to hold on the cloth. With Tyrian purple it is one of the natural vat dyes; woad, named beside them, is another plant that gives the same indigo. Tyrian purple is itself an indigo: 6,6′-dibromoindigo, C16H8Br2N2O2, indigo with two bromine atoms. The vat makes it soluble, and on the fibre, in the air, it turns insoluble again.

  • 8Natural Colorants: Historical, Processing and Sustainable Prospects, 2017
  • 9Microbial Communities Associated With Indigo Fermentation, 2018
  • 10Indian Block-Printed Textiles: Past and Present, 2016
  • 20Block Printing, 2022
  • 21Tyrian purple (PubChem CID 177057)

Red, the alum–alizarin lake

Mordant dyes form complexes with metal mordants, and most give different shades with different mordants. With a red dye such as madder or chay root, an alum mordant gives red and an iron mordant gives black. Indian madder holds high amounts of alizarin, the main compound behind red in most natural dyes; alizarin still needs a mordant such as alum to attach to cotton. Edwards writes that the synthetic form of madder is alizarin, chemically identical to the natural dyestuff but far cheaper. Sources differ on how much alizarin Indian madder holds: the GI records for Bagru and Sanganeri name purpurin beside it, and the Met finds India’s red dyes chemically different from dyer’s madder.

  • 1GI Journal No. 188: Kutch Ajrakh, 2023
  • 8Natural Colorants: Historical, Processing and Sustainable Prospects, 2017
  • 11Ajrakh: From Caste Dress to Catwalk, 2016
  • 27Dyeing cotton fabrics is an ancient Indian art, 1992
  • 31Chintz, eight process samples, Coromandel Coast, c.1919, T.1-1920
  • 32Madder Dye, 2022

Black, iron on tannin

Myrobalan, or harde, a strong tannin from the fruit of the chebulic myrobalan tree, has traditionally been used as a mordant in India. Frater names the dyes of ajrakh's colours as indigo, madder and iron acetate.

  • 10Indian Block-Printed Textiles: Past and Present, 2016
  • 13Indigo in Kutch, India, 2024

White, where the dye never reached

For a piece to be called ajrakh it needs all four colours, blue, red, black and white.

  • 1GI Journal No. 188: Kutch Ajrakh, 2023

The vat, up close

रसायन

टैनिन, लोहा और फिटकरी रंगों को पक्का करते हैं

हरड़ में टैनिक अम्ल की मात्रा अधिक होती है; यह एक आवश्यक पूर्व-रंगबंधक है जो छापे गए रंगबंधकों को सूती कपड़े पर चिपकने में मदद करता है। हरड़ से उपचारित कपड़े पर छापा गया kut गहरा, पक्का चॉकलेटी-काला हो जाता है, क्योंकि लेप का लोहा टैनिक अम्ल के साथ ऑक्सीकृत होता है। लाल रंग उभारने के लिए मजीठ और संश्लेषित एलिज़ारिन, दोनों को रंगबंधक के रूप में फिटकरी चाहिए, और रूपरेखा के प्रतिरोध-लेप का चूना फिटकरी को हटा देता है। नील के कुंड से निकाला गया कपड़ा चटक हरा होता है और रेशों पर रंग से ऑक्सीजन के मिलते ही नीला हो जाता है।

1

Tannin, iron and alum make the colours hold

ChemistryWritten

Myrobalan contains high levels of tannic acid, an essential pre-mordant that aids the adhesion of the printed mordants onto the cotton. Printed on harde-treated cloth, kut develops a deep fast chocolate-black as the iron in the paste, oxidised by the air, binds the tannic acid. Madder and synthetic alizarin both need alum as a mordant to develop red, and lime in the outline resist discharges the alum.

2

From Sindh to Kutch at a king's invitation

HistoryWritten

The origin of ajrakh is traced to Sind, and Rao Bharmalji I of Kutch invited Khatri printers from Sindh and gave them land and freedom from tax. Many Khatri printers descend from Jindha Jiva, who founded Dhamadka in the reign of Rao Bharmal I, and Dhamadka and Khavda became the main centres of ajrakh in Kachchh. Indian cotton fragments of the 11th to 14th century found at Al Fustat in Old Cairo were printed with small blocks in simple patterns that bear a striking similarity to ajrak.

3

Blue, red, black and white, printed both sides

OverviewWritten

Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique of direct and resist printing and dyeing, made by Khatri artisans as a double-sided textile. Its tradition is kept up in the Kutch villages of Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda, and its process and designs are common to Sindh, where it originated, and to Barmer district of Rajasthan. A traditional piece needs all four colours, blue, black, red and white, and the most highly prized cloths were printed identically on both sides.

4

When the river died and the iron rose

Geography and waterWritten

Edwards writes that the River Suran served Dhamadka until the late 1980s, and the GI journal records that its water stream dried up in 1989. After the 2001 earthquake Dhamadka's water held more iron, which saddens dye colours, and even one percent of iron leaves black spots on myrobalan-dyed cloth. Ajrakhpur was chosen for good quality groundwater, but its water table is going down and excess iron and rising salinity threaten the craft again.

5

From barter with herders to running yardage

EconomicsWritten

Khatri printers knew their clients through hereditary relationships and bartered their dyed cloth directly with them for milk, animals and grain. Khatri printers of Kutch have almost stopped printing ajrakh for Maldharis, who buy cheaper screen-printed cloth in chemical dyes, mostly from Pakistan and from Khavda. In 2014 Abduljabbar M. Khatri's workshop made 70,000 m of running cotton yardage for Fabindia, one of his largest clients with Maiwa.

6

Balance, order and the priest-king's cloud motif

DesignWritten

Ajrakh design follows mizan, the Islamic principle of balance and order, with the design square divided into quarters and then sixteen parts. A fixed layout sets a large central body of a repeated motif on a tight grid within borders and end panels. Block printers identify the trefoil on the Mohenjo-daro priest-king's shawl with kakar, the cloud motif of ajrakh.

7

Camel dung, myrobalan and lime prepare the cloth

ProcessWritten

The cloth is first scoured in saaj by repeated soaking in castor oil, soda ash and camel dung and drying until it is soft and white, though sources differ on whether these ingredients are still used. In kasanu it is treated with harda (myrobalan), and the white outlines are then printed with rekh blocks in a resist of gum arabic and lime. Kat prints the black with an iron paste, and kan or pa prints a paste of alum and tamarind seed powder where red is required.
